concept.name: Linked List Patterns

relationships.description: Connects Linked List Patterns to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Linked lists trade O(1) random indexing and CPU cache locality for O(1) pointer-based splicing, reversal, and eviction without shifting contiguous memory.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use sentinel dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and HashMap+Doubly-Linked-List hybrids (LRU) to eliminate edge-case bugs and achieve O(1) structural mutations.

concept.whyItMatters: While contiguous arrays (`std::vector`, `ArrayList`) win 95% of general-purpose workloads due to 64-byte CPU cache lines, linked-list patterns remain indispensable wherever O(1) middle removal/promotion is required without reallocation—powering OS kernel intrusive lists (`list_head`), O(1) LRU/LFU caches, Redis Sorted Set skip lists, and lock-free concurrent stacks/queues.
whenToUse: O(1) eviction and recency promotion in LRU/LFU caches by pairing a HashMap (key → node pointer) with a Doubly Linked List.
In-place structural splicing, merging sorted streams, or O(1) head/tail queue operations when the node pointer is already known.
Intrusive kernel/systems structures (e.g., Linux `struct list_head`, timer wheels) and probabilistic Skip Lists (Redis `zset`) requiring lock-friendly or zero-reallocation inserts.
whenNotToUse: Random access by index (`list[i]`) or binary search—O(N) traversal and pointer chasing destroy performance.
Cache-sensitive tight loops or small-element collections (<1,000 items), where `ArrayList`/`vector` beats linked lists by 10–50x due to L1/L2 hardware prefetching.
Memory-constrained environments storing tiny payloads (e.g., 4-byte ints), where 64-bit `prev`/`next` pointers add 16 bytes (400% overhead) per node.
keyPoints: Dummy / Sentinel Head Pattern: prepending a fixed dummy node (`dummy.next = head`) eliminates null-pointer branches when inserting or deleting at the head.
Fast & Slow Pointers (Floyd's Tortoise & Hare): advancing `slow` by 1 and `fast` by 2 finds the midpoint, detects cycles in O(N) time / O(1) space, and locates the cycle entry node.
HashMap + Doubly Linked List (LRU Cache): the map provides O(1) lookup to the node, while `prev`/`next` pointers unlink and move any node to the MRU head in O(1).
Skip Lists (Layered Linked Lists): adding probabilistic express lanes (p = 0.25, max 32 levels in Redis `zset`) upgrades search/insert/delete from O(N) to O(log N) without tree rotations.
CPU Cache & Pointer-Chasing Penalty: each non-contiguous node dereference risks an L1/L2 miss (~100 ns DRAM fetch vs ~1 ns sequential array read).

examples.title: O(1) API Rate-Limiter & Session LRU Cache
examples.scenario: An edge gateway caches 500,000 active TLS session tickets in RAM and must evict the least recently used ticket on every insert in <1 µs.
examples.outcome: Combining a HashMap with a Doubly Linked List using sentinel `head` and `tail` nodes performs `get()` and `put()` (unlink + move-to-head + evict tail) in strictly O(1) pointer swaps with zero array shifting.

examples.title: Redis Sorted Set (`zset`) Leaderboard via Skip List
examples.scenario: A gaming backend maintains a live 10M-player leaderboard supporting `ZADD`, `ZREM`, and `ZRANGE` rank queries under high concurrency.
examples.outcome: Redis pairs a hash table with a 32-level Skip List (`ZSKIPLIST_P = 0.25`), delivering O(log N) score lookups and O(1) sequential range iteration without AVL/Red-Black rebalancing locks.

tradeOffs.factor: Doubly Linked List vs. Contiguous Dynamic Array (`ArrayList`/`vector`)
tradeOffs.pro: O(1) removal/splicing given a node reference and zero periodic `O(N)` resize-and-copy pauses.
tradeOffs.con: 2x–4x higher memory footprint from 8–16 byte pointers plus allocator headers, and 10x slower linear iteration from cache misses.

tradeOffs.factor: Singly Linked List vs. Doubly Linked List
tradeOffs.pro: Singly linked lists cut pointer overhead in half (one `next` pointer) and simplify lock-free CAS stacks (Treiber stack).
tradeOffs.con: Deleting a node given only its pointer requires O(N) traversal to find the predecessor (unless using the copy-next-and-delete trick, which fails on the tail).

tradeOffs.factor: Skip List vs. Balanced BST (Red-Black / AVL)
tradeOffs.pro: Skip Lists require no tree rotations on insert/delete, making range scans trivial and concurrent lock-free/fine-grained locking far simpler.
tradeOffs.con: Higher average pointer memory per node (~1.33 pointers at p=0.25) and probabilistic rather than worst-case O(log N) bounds.

failureModes.name: Lost Reference / Broken Chain During In-Place Reversal
failureModes.description: Overwriting `curr.next = prev` before saving `nxt = curr.next` drops the remainder of the list, causing silent data loss or a null-pointer crash.
failureModes.mitigation: Always capture `nxt = curr.next` as the first line inside the reversal loop before mutating `curr.next`.

failureModes.name: ABA Problem in Lock-Free CAS Lists
failureModes.description: Thread 1 reads head `A`, pauses; Thread 2 pops `A`, pops `B`, and pushes `A` back. Thread 1's `CAS(&head, A, B)` succeeds even though `B` was freed.
failureModes.mitigation: Use versioned/tagged pointers (64-bit pointer + 64-bit monotonic counter via `cmpxchg16b`) or hazard pointers / epoch-based reclamation.

failureModes.name: Sentinel / Null-Head Edge-Case Crash
failureModes.description: Deleting the only node in a 1-element list or merging an empty list triggers `NullPointerException` / segfault when `head` mutates.
failureModes.mitigation: Anchor operations with a dummy sentinel node (`dummy = Node(0, head)`) and return `dummy.next`.

failureModes.name: Cycle-Induced Infinite Loop
failureModes.description: A corrupted `tail.next` pointer (or unvalidated cyclic input) traps traversal loops forever, pegging CPU at 100%.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Floyd's fast/slow cycle check when ingesting untrusted lists and explicitly null-terminate `tail.next = null` after splits.

commonMistakes: Reaching for a LinkedList in Java/C++ thinking it is faster than `ArrayList`/`std::vector` for sequential iteration or small insertions—CPU cache locality almost always favors contiguous arrays.
Forgetting to update both `prev` and `next` pointers (and `head`/`tail` sentinels) when unlinking a node from a doubly linked list.
Writing separate `if (head == null)` and `if (curr == head)` branches instead of using a dummy sentinel node.
Using `head.next.next` in fast/slow loops without checking `fast != null && fast.next != null` first.
Forgetting to break the `next` link (`mid_prev.next = null`) when splitting a list for Merge Sort, causing infinite recursion.

sections.content:
## The idea

A linked list stores elements in heap-allocated nodes chained by explicit memory pointers (`next`, and optionally `prev`) rather than contiguous array indices. That indirection sacrifices $O(1)$ random indexing and CPU cache prefetching in exchange for **$O(1)$ structural mutation**: once you hold a pointer to a node, you can insert, unlink, reverse, or splice sublists in constant time without moving any other element in memory. Nearly all production and interview linked-list algorithms reduce to five core patterns: **sentinel dummy nodes**, **fast/slow pointers**, **in-place pointer reversal**, **HashMap + Doubly Linked List (LRU)**, and **multi-level Skip Lists**.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace **K-Group / In-Place Reversal** (`1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → null`) using a dummy sentinel:
1. **Anchor**: Create `dummy.next = 1`; set `prev = null`, `curr = 1`.
2. **Save & Flip**: Save `nxt = curr.next` (`2`), set `curr.next = prev` (`1 → null`), advance `prev = 1`, `curr = 2`.
3. **Iterate**: Repeat for `2`, `3`, `4`. At termination, `curr == null` and `prev` points to `4` (`4 → 3 → 2 → 1 → null`).
4. **O(1) Space**: Only 3 pointer variables (`prev`, `curr`, `nxt`) are allocated regardless of whether the list holds 4 nodes or 40 million nodes.

sections.content:
## Core Patterns & Systems Primitives

- **Fast & Slow Pointers**: `slow` moves 1 step, `fast` moves 2 steps. Detects cycles in $O(N)$ time / $O(1)$ space; resetting one pointer to `head` and advancing both by 1 finds the exact cycle-entry node.
- **Two-Pointer Gap ($N$-th from End)**: Advance `fast` by $N$ steps first, then advance `slow` and `fast` together until `fast.next == null`.
- **Intrusive Lists (Linux `list_head`)**: Instead of a node wrapping data, the `list_head` struct (`prev`, `next`) is embedded *inside* the target struct and recovered via `container_of()`, eliminating separate node `malloc` calls.
- **Skip Lists**: Multi-level forward pointers (`level[0..31]`) allow $O(\log N)$ search and lock-free concurrent updates.

## Pattern Complexity & Memory Comparison

| Pattern / Structure | Lookup | Insert / Delete (at pointer) | Extra Space | Cache Locality |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Singly Linked List** | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ (after prev) | 1 ptr/node (8 B) | Poor (heap-scattered) |
| **Doubly Linked List** | $O(N)$ | $O(1)$ (any node) | 2 ptrs/node (16 B) | Poor |
| **HashMap + DLL (LRU)** | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ | Map + 2 ptrs/node | Mixed (hash + heap) |
| **Skip List (p=0.25)** | $O(\log N)$ | $O(\log N)$ | ~1.33 ptrs/node | Moderate |
| **Dynamic Array (baseline)** | $O(1)$ | $O(N)$ middle shift | 0 ptrs/item | Excellent (64 B cache line) |

## Failure modes

1. **Null-Pointer Dereference on Edge Inputs**: Empty lists (`head == null`), 1-node lists, or deleting the tail break unguarded `curr.next.next` expressions.
2. **Dangling / Leaked Cycles**: Splitting a list for Merge Sort or cycle removal without explicitly setting `prev.next = null` causes infinite recursion or memory leaks.
3. **Concurrent ABA Corruption**: Lock-free stacks using raw pointer CAS reuse freed addresses, corrupting `head` unless tagged pointers or hazard pointers are used.

## Cache-Conscious Alternatives in Production

In latency-critical C++/Rust/Java systems, pure node-per-element linked lists are often replaced by **unrolled linked lists** (each node stores a 64-byte or 4 KB array chunk of 8–64 items) or **intrusive arena-allocated lists** (nodes stored in a flat `Vec<Node>` addressed by `uint32` indices). This preserves $O(1)$ splicing while keeping data inside L1/L2 CPU cache lines and cutting allocator fragmentation.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Always wrap head-mutating operations with a dummy sentinel node (`dummy.next = head`).
- [ ] Guard fast-pointer advances with `while fast is not None and fast.next is not None`.
- [ ] Save `nxt = curr.next` before overwriting `curr.next` during in-place reversals.
- [ ] Test against 0-node, 1-node, 2-node, and cyclic inputs.
- [ ] Prefer contiguous arrays or unrolled/arena lists unless you genuinely need $O(1)$ mid-list splicing or pointer stability.

interviewProblems.title: Linked List Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Linked List Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Linked lists trade O(1) random indexing and CPU cache locality for O(1) pointer-based splicing, reversal, and eviction without shifting contiguous memory.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Doubly Linked Nodes applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Sentinel Tail (LRU).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Sentinel Tail (LRU) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Always capture `nxt = curr.next` as the first line inside the reversal loop before mutating `curr.next`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use sentinel dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and HashMap+Doubly-Linked-List hybrids (LRU) to eliminate edge-case bugs and achieve O(1) structural mutations.

Avoid trap: Reaching for a LinkedList in Java/C++ thinking it is faster than `ArrayList`/`std::vector` for sequential iteration or small insertions—CPU cache locality almost always favors contiguous arrays.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to update both `prev` and `next` pointers (and `head`/`tail` sentinels) when unlinking a node from a doubly linked list.
When to reach for it: O(1) eviction and recency promotion in LRU/LFU caches by pairing a HashMap (key → node pointer) with a Doubly Linked List.
When to reach for it: In-place structural splicing, merging sorted streams, or O(1) head/tail queue operations when the node pointer is already known.

putItTogether.title: Putting Linked List Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Use sentinel dummy heads, fast/slow pointers, and HashMap+Doubly-Linked-List hybrids (LRU) to eliminate edge-case bugs and achieve O(1) structural mutations.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Linked List Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Combining a HashMap with a Doubly Linked List using sentinel `head` and `tail` nodes performs `get()` and `put()` (unlink + move-to-head + evict tail) in strictly O(1) pointer swaps with zero array shifting.
